concepts.title: Structure of a Neuron and Nerve Impulse Transmission

questions.q: Name the parts of a neuron.
questions.a: Cell body with nucleus, branching dendrites that receive signals, and a long axon ending in axon terminals.

questions.q: How does a nerve impulse travel within a neuron?
questions.a: As an electrical signal: dendrites pick it up, it runs along the axon, and chemicals pass it to the next cell at the synapse.

questions.q: What happens at a synapse?
questions.a: On reaching the axon end, chemicals are released that cross the gap and start a fresh electrical impulse in the next neuron.

questions.q: What is a reflex action? Give two examples.
questions.a: A quick, automatic response to a stimulus without thinking - e.g. jerking the hand from a hot object, or blinking at sudden light.

questions.q: What is a reflex arc?
questions.a: The shortest path of the impulse: receptor -> sensory neuron -> spinal cord -> motor neuron -> effector muscle.

questions.q: Why does the reflex arc bypass the brain?
questions.a: For speed: the spinal cord handles the response at once while the brain is informed later - thinking would be too slow.

concepts.title: Regions and Functions of the Human Brain

questions.q: Name the three main regions of the brain and one job of each.
questions.a: Forebrain (thinking, memory), midbrain (involuntary reflexes of eye/head), hindbrain with medulla (heartbeat, breathing, balance).

questions.q: Which part of the brain maintains posture and balance?
questions.a: The cerebellum in the hindbrain.

questions.q: Which activities does the medulla control?
questions.a: Involuntary vital actions like heartbeat, breathing, blood pressure, vomiting and salivation.

concepts.title: Protection of the Central Nervous System

questions.q: How is the brain protected in the body?
questions.a: It sits in a bony skull and is wrapped in three membranes (meninges) with cerebrospinal fluid cushioning shocks.

questions.q: How is the spinal cord protected?
questions.a: It runs inside the vertebral column (backbone), which guards it like the skull guards the brain.

questions.q: Why is cerebrospinal fluid important?
questions.a: It acts as a shock absorber between the delicate CNS tissue and the bone, and also nourishes it.

questions.q: How does a muscle move a bone?
questions.a: A nerve impulse makes the muscle fibres shorten; the muscle pulls (never pushes) the bone at its joint.

questions.q: Why must muscles work in pairs, like the biceps and triceps?
questions.a: Muscles can only pull; one muscle bends the joint while its partner straightens it back.

questions.q: What triggers the chemical change that shortens a muscle fibre?
questions.a: A nerve impulse arriving at the muscle cell sets off chemical changes that make the fibre contract.

questions.q: What is the immediate response of a plant to touch, as in mimosa?
questions.a: Cells of the leaf base change shape by losing/gaining water, so the leaf droops at once - no growth involved.

questions.q: Why is touch response in plants not a reflex-like nerve action?
questions.a: Plants have no nerve cells; the signal spreads cell to cell as a chemical that changes cell water content.

questions.q: Do immediate plant movements involve growth? Why?
questions.a: No - they are quick shape changes of existing cells, unlike growth movements which take days.

questions.q: What is phototropism? Which hormone causes it?
questions.a: Growth of a shoot towards light, caused by auxin collecting on the shaded side making that side elongate more.

questions.q: Name the plant movements called geotropism and hydrotropism.
questions.a: Roots growing downward in response to gravity (geotropism) and toward water (hydrotropism).

questions.q: How does a tendril coil around a support?
questions.a: Touch makes auxin gather on the far side, so that side grows faster and the tendril curls around the support.

questions.q: Name any three plant hormones and one function each.
questions.a: Auxin (cell elongation), gibberellin (stem growth, fruiting), cytokinin (cell division), abscisic acid (wilting, dormancy).

questions.q: Which plant hormone promotes wilting and dormancy?
questions.a: Abscisic acid - it inhibits growth and helps the plant face stress.

questions.q: Which hormone would you spray to make fruits ripen or drop leaves?
questions.a: Ethylene speeds fruit ripening; abscisic acid promotes leaf fall.

questions.q: What are endocrine glands?
questions.a: Ductless glands that pour hormones straight into blood, e.g. thyroid, pituitary, adrenal, pancreas (islets).

questions.q: How do hormones reach their target organs?
questions.a: They are carried by blood to all body parts but only the target organs with matching receptors respond.

questions.q: Name the hormone that lowers blood sugar and its gland.
questions.a: Insulin, secreted by the pancreas.

questions.q: How is thyroid hormone secretion kept in check?
questions.a: Feedback: low blood thyroxine signals the pituitary to release TSH; once thyroxine is enough, TSH release stops.

questions.q: What disease follows iodine deficiency and why?
questions.a: Goitre - without iodine the thyroid cannot make thyroxine, so it swells trying to.

questions.q: Why is adrenaline called the emergency hormone?
questions.a: In fear or stress the adrenal glands release adrenaline that speeds heartbeat and breathing, readying the body for action.
